text: A chart plots a whole series of values. Sometimes that's more than you need — sometimes you just want one number, and a quick read on whether it's good, bad, or somewhere in between. That's exactly what a gauge is for.

A Gauge data region displays a single aggregated value from your dataset — full stop. Every gauge lives inside a gauge panel, the top-level container, and you can put more than one gauge in a panel if you want them sharing filtering, grouping, and sorting. This illustration labels the parts you'll be setting properties on: the Gauge Frame around the outside, the Scale with its Major and Minor Tick Marks and Scale Labels, the Range shaded across part of the dial, and the Pointer itself — here a needle style, with a Pointer Value and a Pointer Cap where it's anchored. Learn these names now, because the property dialogs you'll open later assume you already know them.

Reporting Services gives you exactly two gauge types, and radial is the one people picture first. It's circular, it resembles a speedometer, and its pointer is usually a needle — though you can swap in a marker or a bar instead. Reach for a radial gauge when the value genuinely reads like a dial: a velocity, a percentage of capacity, anything where "how far around the circle" is an intuitive read.

The second type is linear — rectangular, horizontal or vertical, with a pointer that's usually styled like a thermometer. Same job as a radial gauge, different shape, and that shape difference actually matters: because it's rectangular, a linear gauge fits neatly inside a table or matrix cell to show per-row progress, in a way a circular gauge just can't. Whichever type you pick, remember Reporting Services will not set the scale's minimum and maximum for you — it has no way to know what "full" means for your data, so that's on you to define explicitly, or the gauge has no real context at all.
Next lesson, we go even simpler — indicators, which are really just gauges with the frame and pointer stripped down to a single icon.
